title: any()
summary: True if at least one element is truthy — short-circuiting on the first hit.
description: Pairs with `all`. Both stop as soon as the answer is known, so passing a generator expression means you may not evaluate the whole sequence.
returns: True or False. False for an empty iterable.

examples.title: With a generator expression
examples.code:
rows = [{'error': None}, {'error': 'timeout'}]
print(any(r['error'] for r in rows))

examples.title: It short-circuits
examples.code:
def check(n):
    print('checked', n)
    return n > 1

print(any(check(n) for n in [1, 2, 3]))

real_world_usage: Validation ('did anything fail?'), permission checks, and replacing a loop with a flag variable.

common_mistakes.fix: The list comprehension evaluates everything first, defeating the short circuit. Drop the brackets to pass a generator.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting any() to return the matching element
common_mistakes.fix: It returns a bool. Use next((x for x in xs if cond(x)), None) for the element.

performance_notes: O(n) worst case, often much less thanks to short-circuiting — provided you pass a lazy iterable.
